opening.headline: When there's no baseline to judge whether a structure is sufficient given numerous requirements, you learn how to select a structure based on predictability and failure costs.
body: When multiple requirements accumulate—such as order status updates, data investigations, code modifications, and refund processing upon errors—the most dazzling architecture becomes appealing. However, there is no clear benchmark to determine whether a single call, a workflow, a single agent, or a multi-agent system is sufficient.

Anthropic recommends finding the simplest possible solution and adding complexity only when necessary. In this course, we create two axes for judging when complexity is needed and a structure selection matrix, then apply it to the tasks of order processing, research, and code modification, establishing appropriate structures with clear rationale.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Structural candidates can be compared based on predictability and failure cost.
We can provide the rationale for selecting the simplest structure that satisfies the requirements.

screens.title: The requirements are numerous but there are no standards.
screens.lead: We have a scenario where four requirements are stacked upon a single service. Expand each item to verify the components required by the candidate architecture.

visual.alt: A diagram showing three requirement cards and four candidate structure boxes connected by question mark lines.
labels: Refund processing in case of error

items.title: Single LLM call
items.body: One LLM call refined with search and context-based examples. The only required components are the prompt and search. Anthropic states that this level is sufficient for many applications. Requirements such as informing about order status are adequately addressed by this structure.

items.title: workflow
items.body: This is a structure where code determines the path, similar to chaining, routing, and parallelization. The required components are code that connects stages and checks between stages. It provides predictability and consistency in well-defined operations.

items.title: Single agent
items.body: The model involves looping over tools. Required components include termination conditions such as tool definitions and loop bounds. While suitable for open-ended tasks where a predefined path cannot be established, it accumulates costs and errors over time.

items.title: Multi-agent
items.body: This is a structure involving multiple agents and their coordination. The required components are subordinate agents, delegation instructions, and result composition. Token expansion up to approximately 15 times the chat length is only justified when parallelism and context isolation are absolutely necessary.

screens.outro: Without a basis, selection tends to result in the most dazzling structure. First, let's examine your system.

screens.title: Think of components that can be removed
screens.lead: After first thinking through the question mentally and making a choice, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Answers are not entered or submitted.

items.prompt: What components can be removed from the current system?
items.answer: At first, it seems like all components are necessary. By gradually removing elements and checking which requirements are broken, you'll discover what is truly essential. The structure choice in this course asks not about what to add, but rather what can be removed.

items.prompt: If that component is absent, which requirement would be violated?
items.answer: If a requirement cannot be said to be broken down, then its components have not been proven to be necessary. For example, if removing a subordinate agent does not change the outcome, then that agent merely incurs cost without providing value.

items.prompt: Can you directly view the prompts and responses hidden by the framework?
items.answer: Anthropic states that frameworks may make debugging difficult by abstracting layers, thereby hiding prompts and responses. If the internal workings are not visible, it becomes hard to determine whether the structure is truly necessary. Using systems with an understanding of their internal operations is fundamental.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the two axes for structuring.

screens.title: Two axes that define structure: predictability and failure cost
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the underlined terms in the text, a brief description appears. Read how the two axes are used in structure selection.

visual.alt: The horizontal axis represents predictability of the path, and the vertical axis represents failure cost, resulting in a grid layout that fits well within the four quadrants.
labels: Path is not known in advance
Reducing agent autonomy by adding approvals and sandboxes

data.text: When determining the structure, ask two key questions first. The first is predictability. If you know the path in advance, the workflow gains consistency. If you don't know the path and continuous judgment is required, agents provide flexibility. The second is Failure cost. If the cost of error is high, reduce autonomy and add Gate and approvals, as well as sandbox. An agent's autonomy increases costs and error accumulation, making it suitable for scaling in trusted environments. Google Cloud's architecture guide separates designs into single-agent and multi-agent architectures based on use cases. OpenAI documentation advises selecting the execution environment based on required Control level and responsibility for state management.

terms.tip: This indicates the extent to which the steps and order of work are known in advance. The higher this level, the better suited it is for a workflow that defines paths through code.
The magnitude of losses caused by improper actions, including money, trust, and irreversible changes.
This is the point where the program checks intermediate results to decide whether to proceed to the next step.
This describes a method for running in an isolated environment to ensure that failure impacts do not spread outside. Agents are recommended to undergo sufficient testing within this environment.
The extent to which an agent's loop and state are directly managed. Managed services require less effort but offer greater control when configured directly.

screens.outro: We will combine both axes into a single budget of complexity and create a selection matrix.

screens.title: Complexity Budget and Structure Selection Table
screens.lead: Complexity is a budget that decreases the more you have. Read the table below from top to bottom to confirm the order of structure, from simple to complex, and the conditions required at each stage.

data.caption: Selection table for structure based on requirements (simplest form)
rows: A single LLM call accompanied by search and examples
Many applications are sufficient here, so let's begin with this structure.
Sub-operation is fixed or input type is split or independent operation exists
Subtasks that cannot be predetermined must be divided based on input.
The path is open, so the model must select the next action at each step.
Cost, delay, and error accumulation increases

data.notes: Agent SDK, Agents SDK, selecting a platform such as a managed agent involves the following steps after defining the structure. First, define the structure, then choose the tools to implement it. As you progress to each subsequent stage, you must justify the increased complexity with a single sentence explaining why you moved up. As you move down the table, more decisions are delegated to the model, while the code takes on fewer guarantees. Therefore, each time, first verify whether the same result can be achieved at a simpler stage. If no benefit is observed at a higher stage, it is a valid choice to revert back to a previous stage. Remember that the stages in the table represent cost order, not hierarchy. Additionally, it is natural to apply different stages across various workflows within a single system. For example, order processing can be two stages, while research may require three or more stages—these do not contradict each other.

screens.outro: Since we have learned how to read tables, I will now provide an example by specifying the reading order for three tasks.

screens.title: Look at the table for three tasks: how to read
screens.lead: Select each tab to review the characteristics of the three tasks. The decision is made with rationale on the following explanation screen.

tabs.label: Task 1: Order processing
tabs.body: Order receipt, inventory check, payment, and shipping request always proceed in the same sequence. The path is predictable. In contrast, payment errors or duplicate orders incur high failure costs. A combination with high predictability and significant failure costs.

tabs.label: Task 2 Research
tabs.body: The specific sub-questions required depend on the topic raised by the user. The exploration path is open and the scope is broad. There may be a large volume of material to read, making it difficult to fit within a single context. While there is a risk of providing incorrect information, the risk of irreversible actions is rare.

tabs.label: Task 3 Code Modification
tabs.body: You may not know in advance how many files need to be changed. Instead, you can run tests to verify the results. The outcomes obtained in the environment serve as evidence for each step. The number of independent tasks that can be divided for parallel processing is relatively smaller than research.

tabs.label: Reading order
tabs.body: The decision follows four questions in this order: Can the path be known in advance? Is the failure cost high? Can the context be confined to a single location? Are there independent tasks that need to be performed in parallel? If the answer to the first question is determined, the subsequent questions can be omitted.

screens.outro: Now we will explain the process of comparing the structures of these three tasks based on their foundations.

screens.title: Explanation: Rationale for selecting the structure of order processing, research, and code modification
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates the process of selecting three tasks and organizing them in the matrix to determine the structure. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Order Processing 1: Gate in the Workflow
steps.body: Order processing involves fixed stages with high error costs. The two-stage selection form and fixed subtask workflow align well. Gates are placed between each stage to validate critical values—such as inventory quantities or payment amounts—that must not be incorrect, using code-based checks. Additionally, the option of adding an approval stage to irreversible payment stages is also considered.

steps.title: Order Processing 2: The agent is not used
steps.body: An agent's autonomy is not necessary for this task. The path is already predetermined, so the model has no choice to make. Instead, autonomy incurs only costs, delays, and accumulated errors. Classifying user queries or generating guidance statements in natural language can be adequately handled with a single call within a stage.

steps.title: Research 1: Orchestrator-Worker
steps.body: Research breaks down into sub-questions that vary depending on the input. Since it's impossible to pre-determine which sub-questions are needed, a three-stage orchestrator-worker system in a selection matrix is appropriate. The central component analyzes the query, decomposes it into sub-tasks, and then synthesizes the results. Anthropic's research system implements this architecture.

steps.title: Research 2: Exploration is separated into a subordinate agent
steps.body: The search scope is broad and may result in reading material exceeding a single context. Therefore, the search component is separated into subordinate agents, each of which reads within its own context and returns only the key insights. Both parallelism and context isolation are clearly justified, making it valid to use part of the five-stage multi-agent system. However, a single agent is sufficient for simple fact verification.

steps.title: Code Change 1: Start with a single-agent loop
steps.body: While it's uncertain how many files need to be modified, the results can be validated through testing. Since the outcomes obtained in the environment form an open pathway, we begin with the four-step agent loop: the model reads a file, modifies it, runs a test, observes the results, and then makes a reevaluation.

steps.title: Code Change 2: Multi-agent is delayed
steps.body: Code modifications involve fewer independent tasks than research, with high interdependencies between them. Due to the small benefit gained by multi-agent systems, adoption is discouraged. Instead, loops are equipped with a maximum number of iterations and a cost upper bound. These are minimal safety mechanisms to prevent the risk of infinite looping.

steps.title: The common points of the three conclusions
steps.body: All three tasks began at the lowest level of the selection scale and only advanced when a need was clearly established. Order processing did not advance at all, research advanced only where a clear justification existed, and code modification advanced only as far as the agent loop due to open pathways.

steps.title: Read again when requirements change
steps.body: A selection form is not a one-time-use document. When a new requirement is added to the order processing workflow—such as "the customer can freely express dissatisfaction, and then the situation is understood and responded to"—only that specific part becomes an open-process task. Even in this case, the entire workflow is not converted into an agent; instead, only the open portion is separated into an agent call, while the fixed stages before and after remain unchanged. Requirements must always be understood and applied at a granular, partial level.

steps.title: Instructor's decision summary
steps.body: When summarized in a single table, the comparisons become straightforward. Order processing involves a workflow with a gate, research uses an orchestrator-worker setup with exploration separation, and code modification follows a single-agent loop with a ceiling. Regardless of the decision, the rationale emerges from two dimensions: whether the path was known in advance, and the cost of error. Our system's response begins with the same two questions. When documenting decisions, include not only the chosen architecture but also the ones not selected and the reasons for excluding them. This provides a basis for determining at which stage future requirements might need to be escalated. Particularly, documenting "why an agent was not used" eliminates the need to reiterate the same discussion.

screens.outro: We will conclude by summarizing the decision-making approach in one sentence.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Start simply, and introduce complexity only when it's proven necessary.
screens.lead: We organize the criteria for determining structure.

paragraphs: The structure starts simple and adds complexity only when necessity is proven. Complexity comes at the cost of shrinking budgets. With each additional component, costs, delays, and debugging difficulties increase. Therefore, there must be a one-sentence justification for adding anything.

The two axes that define structural candidates are whether the path is known in advance—workflow if known, agent if not known. If failure costs are high, autonomy is reduced, and additional elements such as gates, approvals, and sandboxes are introduced. The platform and SDK determine this structure and then implement it.

The final question of this course is one: up to what point is the current structure of my system necessary, and where does it become unproven or unnecessary? If there are components that can be removed without breaking requirements, then that represents a reduction in complexity. There's no need to overhaul everything right now; it's sufficient simply to ask this question whenever a proposal to add new components arises. Decisions to simplify the structure are part of the design process, and they should be concluded by verifying that the requirements are still fully satisfied after simplification. Regularly repeating this review helps prevent the system from gradually becoming heavier over time.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: A good design is not the most elaborate one, but the simplest structure that satisfies requirements.

glossary.def: This indicates the extent to which the steps and order of work are known in advance. The higher this value, the better the workflow fits.
The loss caused by improper behavior. The more such losses, the less autonomy is granted and the more safeguards are implemented.
It is a limited resource used whenever components are added to the structure. Use it only where necessity has been proven.
A table showing how requirements and constraints are addressed in a single call, workflow, agent, and multi-agent systems.

misconceptions.myth: The more requirements there are, the more complex the structure should be.
misconceptions.fact: The simplest structure that satisfies the requirements is preferred. Even if the requirements are extensive, they are mostly resolved by fixed-path workflows or a single call.

misconceptions.myth: Multi-agent systems offer the most scalable predefined solution.
misconceptions.fact: Context isolation and parallelism are only justified when necessary and incur high token costs. The benefits are minimal for tasks that rarely require parallelization.

misconceptions.myth: Choosing a platform determines its structure.
misconceptions.fact: First, define the structure and then select the tool to implement it. The platform does not decide the structure on your behalf.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Start with a simple structure and add complexity only when it is proven necessary.
Compare structure candidates based on predictability and failure costs.
Complexity should be justified only by proven necessity and within budget.
First, define the architecture, then choose the SDK or platform.

checks.q: When establishing a structure for a task with high failure costs, what is the most appropriate approach?
options: Enhances the agent's autonomy to its maximum level, enabling it to recover on its own.
It reduces autonomy and adds gates, approvals, and sandboxes.
Divides it into multiple agents and has them verify each other.
Introduce the framework to hide the prompt
checks.explain: Path predictability and failure cost are the two axes that define a system's structure. Higher failure cost leads to reduced autonomy and increased control mechanisms.

wrong.0: The higher the autonomy, the greater the accumulated cost and error risk, making it unsuitable for tasks with high failure costs.
wrong.2: Increasing agents does not enhance control; it only increases tuning and costs.
wrong.3: The abstraction of the framework may obscure prompts and responses, making debugging difficult.

checks.q: What is the most appropriate structure for research tasks that dynamically change based on input and have a broad search scope, potentially exceeding context limits?

checks.explain: If the child tasks cannot be anticipated in advance, the orchestrator-worker model is appropriate; if the search space is broad and context may overflow, consider decomposing it into subordinate agents for isolation and protection.
